probe.sample: 乐启享 THEME Noether's Theorem Every continuous symmetry of a physical system's action gives rise to a corresponding conserved quantity. 01. THE CORE INSIGHT Symmetry Breeds Conservation Emmy Noether proved in 1918 that for every continuous symmetry of a system's action 𝑆 = ∫ 𝐿 𝑑 𝑡 , there exists an associated quantity that does not change with time. The symmetry condition is that the Lagrangian changes by at most a total time derivative under an infinitesimal transformation 𝑞 𝑖 → 𝑞 𝑖 + 𝜖 𝛿 𝑞 𝑖 : 𝛿 𝐿 = 𝑑 𝐹 𝑑 𝑡 ⟹ 𝑄 = ∑ 𝑖 𝜕 𝐿 𝜕 𝑞 ˙ 𝑖 𝛿 𝑞 𝑖 − 𝐹 = const The conserved quantity 𝑄 is called the Noether charge. The three great examples: time-translation invariance gives energy; space-translation invariance gives linear momentum; rotational invariance gives angular momentum. REAL WORLD ANALOGY The Rules of a Fair Game Imagine a game whose rules are identical no matter when you play (time symmetry) — your score total is always preserved. If the rules are identical wherever you play (space symmetry) — momentum is preserved. If identical in every direction you face (rotational symmetry) — angular momentum is preserved. Noether showed physics is the ultimate fair game. SYMMETRY TYPE TIME TRANSLATION Symmetry Breeds Conservation simulation. Symmetry Type: Time Translation. 02. THE NOETHER CHARGE Canonical Momentum & Conserved Quantities The canonical momentum conjugate to coordinate 𝑞 𝑖 is 𝑝 𝑖 = 𝜕 𝐿 / 𝜕 𝑞 ˙ 𝑖 . Under an infinitesimal symmetry transformation 𝛿 𝑞 𝑖 , the Noether charge is: 𝑄 = ∑ 𝑖 𝑝 𝑖 𝛿 𝑞 𝑖 − 𝐹 , 𝑑 𝑄 𝑑 𝑡 = 0 For time translation ( 𝑡 → 𝑡 + 𝜖 ): 𝛿 𝑞 𝑖 = 𝑞 ˙ 𝑖 , 𝐹 = 𝐿 , giving 𝑄 = ∑ 𝑖 𝑝 𝑖 𝑞 ˙ 𝑖 − 𝐿 = 𝐻 — the Hamiltonian (total energy). For spatial translation: 𝛿 𝑥 = 1 , 𝐹 = 0 , giving 𝑄 = 𝑝 𝑥 — linear momentum. For rotation about z: 𝛿 𝑥 = − 𝑦 , 𝛿 𝑦 = 𝑥 , giving 𝑄 = 𝑥 𝑝 𝑦 − 𝑦 𝑝 𝑥 = 𝐿 𝑧 — angular momentum. KEY INSIGHT Beyond Classical Mechanics In quantum field theory, every internal symmetry (e.g., U(1) gauge invariance of electromagnetism) produces a conserved Noether current. Electric charge conservation follows from U(1) symmetry; colour charge from SU(3) symmetry of QCD. Noether's theorem is the invisible scaffolding of the entire Standard Model. probe.head: 乐启享 THEME Principle of Least Action Nature is parsimonious: every physical system evolves along the unique path that makes its action stationary. 01. THE ACTION INTEGRAL Hamilton's Principle The Actio
probe.sample: 乐启享 THEME Principle of Least Action Nature is parsimonious: every physical system evolves along the unique path that makes its action stationary. 01. THE ACTION INTEGRAL Hamilton's Principle The Action ( 𝑆 ) is a single scalar number — the time-integral of the Lagrangian 𝐿 = 𝑇 − 𝑉 along a path between two fixed states. Hamilton's Principle asserts that the path actually taken by a physical system is the one for which the action is stationary ( 𝛿 𝑆 = 0 ): not necessarily a minimum, but an extremum. 𝑆 [ 𝑞 ] = ∫ 𝑡 1 𝑡 2 𝐿 ( 𝑞 𝑖 , 𝑞 ˙ 𝑖 , 𝑡 ) 𝑑 𝑡 , 𝛿 𝑆 = 0 Applying calculus of variations to this condition yields the Euler-Lagrange equations — the equations of motion for any generalized coordinate 𝑞 𝑖 , free of constraint forces. REAL WORLD ANALOGY Fermat's Principle of Light Just as a ray of light always travels the path that minimizes travel time (Fermat's Principle), a particle travels the path that makes mechanical action stationary. Both are instances of the same deep variational logic. GRAVITY (G) 9.8 M/S² LENGTH (L) 1.5 M Hamilton's Principle simulation. Gravity (g) m/s²: 9.8. Length (l) m: 1.5. 02. VARIATIONAL CALCULUS Euler-Lagrange Equations By demanding 𝛿 𝑆 = 0 for all small path variations 𝛿 𝑞 𝑖 ( 𝑡 ) that vanish at the endpoints, integration by parts produces the Euler-Lagrange equations: 𝑑 𝑑 𝑡 ( 𝜕 𝐿 𝜕 𝑞 ˙ 𝑖 ) − 𝜕 𝐿 𝜕 𝑞 𝑖 = 0 These second-order ODEs replace Newton's 𝐹 = 𝑚 𝑎 in any coordinate system. For a free particle ( 𝑉 = 0 ) they give uniform motion; for a pendulum they reproduce the nonlinear swing equation — all from one scalar 𝐿 . KEY INSIGHT Coordinate Independence Because the Lagrangian is a scalar, the Euler-Lagrange equations hold in any generalized coordinates — polar, spherical, or curvilinear — without rewriting force components. Constraints are handled automatically. PATH VARIANTS (N) 5 Euler-Lagrange Equations simulation. Path Variants (n): 5. 03. UNIVERSAL REACH From Classical to Quantum The principle extends far beyond classical mechanics. In optics, Fermat's principle minimizes optical path length. In quantum mechanics, Feynman's path integral formulation sums 𝑒 𝑖 𝑆 / ℏ over all paths — the classical stationary path dominates as ℏ → 0 . In General Relativity, the Einstein–Hilbert action 𝑆 = ∫ 𝑅 − 𝑔 𝑑 4 𝑥 yields Einstein's field equations. probe.sample: 电路组建实验:直流虚拟实验室 电路组建实验:直流虚拟实验室 is an interactive sim. It changes as you play with it. It has a Play Area and a Control Area. In Play Area: A Construction Area creates a building space for components added from a Circuit Component Toolbox. Build and navigate your circuits there. If Voltmeters and Ammeters are out of the toolbox, you can take measurements. In Control Area: Voltmeters and Ammeters can be found in the Sensor Toolbox. Display Options provide ways to add or remove information about components in the Construction Area. There's an option to choose between a Lifelike View or a Schematic View for circuit components, and you can Reset All to clear everything and start over. Currently, Construction Area has no circuit components. Several lifelike components are available in Circuit Components carousel. Add circuit components and start connecting. Be sure to add at least one Wire. This screen has custom interactions. If needed, check out keyboard shortcuts under Sim Resources. Play Area Construction Area Add circuit components and sensors as needed. Then, use connection options to build circuits, measurement options to take measurements, and edit options to adjust component specifications. Use Delete key to snip connections or remove components and sensors. Connected components auto-organize into groups and everything is movable with the Arrow keys. Checkout Keyboard Shortcuts for more handy shortcuts. Circuit Component Toolbox Look for components in carousel and add them to Construction Area. Once added, return to Construction Area and look for components and their connection points to edit or choose options for connecting. probe.sample: Band Structure Band Structure is an interactive sim. It changes as you play with it. It has a Play Area and a Control Area. In Play Area: In the Energy Diagram, a row of up to eight identical potential energy wells is drawn with a ladder of bound energy levels. Draggable handles on the curve change the size of the wells and the distance between them. Energy Diagram Controls set the potential well type, the number of wells, the electric field, and the selected energy level. Below the Energy Diagram, the Quantum State Graph shares its position axis. It plots either the probability density or the wave function for the selected energy level. Wave Function Parts checkboxes choose which parts are plotted. A button in the graph hides or shows the plotted curves. In Control Area: Tool Controls add a Magnifier and a movable Reference Line, and show value labels on the diagram. Time controls restart, play, pause, and step the system through time, set how fast time passes, and show or hide the elapsed time. Reset All returns the simulation to its starting state. ‪Currently,‬ ‪Potential well type is ‪Finite Square‬.‬ ‪Number of wells is 3.‬ ‪Electric field is 0 volts per nanometer.‬ ‪‪Probability Density‬ is displayed for energy level 1.‬ ‪Time is evolving in femtoseconds.‬ Choose the number of wells and step through the energy levels to explore the lattice. This screen has custom interactions. If needed, check out keyboard shortcuts under Sim Resources. probe.head: 绳波 绳波 is an interactive sim. It changes as you play with it. It has a Play Area and a Control Area. In Play Area: Explore the physical properties of waves by manipulating a string that tightly stretch
probe.sample: 绳波 绳波 is an interactive sim. It changes as you play with it. It has a Play Area and a Control Area. In Play Area: Explore the physical properties of waves by manipulating a string that tightly stretches across the play area. Move the string yourself with a wrench, use a continuous oscillator, or pulse the string to generate waves. Every wave mode provides different options to tune the strings' properties and motion, which affects the waves you create and observe. The end of the string can be fixed to the end of the play area, left loose, or removed entirely to extend infinitely. In Control Area: Several tools are available to support measurements of different properties of the resulting waves. Move the wrench or choose another way to start making waves. This screen has custom interactions. If needed, check out keyboard shortcuts under Sim Resources. Play Area Wave Generation Currently, the wrench clamped to the string is near the middle of the play area, and the string is still and flat. The end of the string is fixed to a clamp. Wave Mode Create wave manually, continuously, or with individual pulses. Manual Oscillate Pulse String End Type Set attachment for the end of the string. Fixed End Loose End No End Wrench Move the wrench up and down to drag the string and make a wave. 重新开始 Reset string position to still and flat. Time Controls Pause sim to step through little by little. Pause Step Forward Sim Speeds For closer observations Play sim on slower speed. 正常 慢速 Wave and String Properties Controls to change the properties of the generated wave and the string. 阻尼 Amount of energy lost to the environment. 张力 Amount the string is stretched. Control Area Measurement Tools Tools to visually measure properties of waves. Pause the sim to help make precise measurements. 尺子 Vertical and horizontal rulers to measure distance. 计时器 Stopwatch to measure elapsed time. 参考线 Movable dashed laser line to visually line up with waves to compare amplitude changes. Optionally, a moveable ruler can be used to measure distance between the spheres' centers. In the Control Area, there are options to change force notations and mass representations, and a button to reset the sim. Currently, force on m1 by m2 is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction of force on m2 by m1. probe.sample: 引力实验室：基础 引力实验室：基础 is an interactive sim. It changes as you play with it. It has a Play Area and a Control Area. The Play Area has two mass spheres, a blue sphere labeled mass 1 and a red sphere labeled mass 2. A force arrow starts at the center of each sphere and points directly at the opposite sphere. Spheres can be moved closer or farther from each other along an invisible track. The mass of each sphere can be increased or decreased. Each sphere is held in place by a robot. In the Control Area, checkboxes change what things are shown and how they behave, and a button resets the sim. Currently, force on mass 1 by mass 2 is of equal size and points directly opposite to the force on mass 2 by mass 1. Force arrows are tiny at 33.4 牛. 质量 1 and 质量 2 are close to each other, centers exactly 4 kilometers apart. Mass of 质量 1 is 2 billion kilograms, half the size of 质量 2 at 4 billion kilograms. probe.sample: 目录 煤的综合利用 · 气化 C(s) + H₂O(g) → CO(g) + H₂(g) ΔH = +131.3 kJ·mol⁻¹ 主线问题 煤只能烧吗？怎么把煤变成能造化肥、造甲醇的气？ 运行中 得分 0 检测 Q 玩法 全屏 F 设备名 N 因果链 气化 C + H₂O(g) → CO + H₂，吸热，把煤变成组成可调的气 ↔ 供热 靠烧掉一部分煤供热：氧多则温度高，但更多碳变成 CO₂ → 变换 CO + H₂O ⇌ CO₂ + H₂ 放热可逆；煤气化用耐硫变换，带硫也中毒不了 → 净化 −40 ℃ 甲醇一次吸掉 H₂S 与 CO₂，硫送克劳斯变成硫磺 → 去向 甲醇要 H₂/CO ≈ 2，合成氨要 H₂/N₂ = 3（深变换 + 配氮） 方程式 · 条件 无新反应：这一步只讲「为什么要气化」 气化剂 = 水蒸气 + 氧气；产品气 = CO + H₂（合成气） 煤是混合物 气化是化学变化 产品是合成气 本步 问句 → 动手 → 结论 + 要点 + 考点 ‹ 1 煤挖出来直接烧不是挺好吗，为什么要先变成气？ 整厂 · 五段装置 煤是混合物 气化是化学变化 产品是合成气 动手试一试 还没做 拖动视角绕厂区看一圈：五段装置、五条物料流线，还有一条绕过变换炉的旁路配气管 应该看到：参考工况正在跑：有效气含量 79.5 %、H₂/CO 2.33、碳转化率 94.7 %、总硫 0.1 ppm 揭示结论 复位本步 工段流程 ① 备煤 › ② 气化炉 › ③ 变换 › ④ 净化 › ⑤ 去下游 中控台 拖一个滑块，看全厂的代价 › 有效气含量 0.0 H₂/CO — 碳转化率 — 入炉碳 总硫 — ≤ 1 ppm 氧煤比 O₂/C 教材 0.23–0.3 量程 0.16–0.4 蒸汽煤比 H₂O/C 教材 0.4–0.7 量程 0.2–1 变换炉出口温度 教材 232–450 ℃ 量程 200–450 ℃ 低温甲醇洗脱硫 产品气去向 炉温与有效气—氧煤比 — 炉温 · -- 有效气 · ● 当前 参考工况 开车 ① 备煤制浆 ② 气化炉 ③ 耐硫变换 ④ 净化与硫回收 ⑤ 产品气去向 旁路配气（甲醇路线） H₂ CO 配氮（来自空分） ‹ 上一步 第 1 / 8 步 下一步 › 示意声明：设备造型与管道走向、炉内 4 段温度带、配气比与硫残留为教学示意；热化学数据取自 NIST 与 NETL 资料（详见事实表），读数由课件模型算出。 ← → 翻步 · 点步骤条任一步可跳 · 1–8 跳步 · Esc 回中控台 快捷键 1–8 工步 · Q 检测 · 空格 开停车 · N 设备名 · F 全屏 · Esc 回控制台 步骤 1 为什么气化 2 供热还是供气 3 炉子里长什么样 4 蒸汽多好还是少好 5 变换调比例 6 为什么要脱硫 7 变成什么 8 考核

probe.sample: 目录 金属钠的性质（含钠着火扑救） Na − e⁻ → Na⁺ · 每个钠原子都只失 1 个电子，所以它见氧就变、见水更凶、着火只能盖干砂 主线问题 一块银白色的小金属，为什么必须泡在煤油里，着火时连水都不能浇？ 运行中 得分 0 检测 Q 玩法 全屏 F 设备名 N 因果链 最外层 1 个电子 很容易失去 → 钠是很强的还原剂（教材 p.34） → 见氧就变 常温生成 Na₂O；加热燃烧发出黄色火焰、生成淡黄色 Na₂O₂（p.35） → 见水更凶 2Na + 2H₂O = 2NaOH + H₂↑，剧烈反应、放出热量、溶液显碱性（p.37） → 所以不能用水 水把反应带进来，反应放热又放出可燃的 H₂ → 只能用干砂 Na₂O₂ 与 CO₂ 反应反而放出 O₂（p.37）→ 干砂 / 专用灭火剂 方程式 · 条件 Na − e⁻ → Na⁺ 四个站位 · 一张实验台 · 全程不换场景 最外层 1 个电子 四个站位 0.0 mmol 本步 问句 → 动手 → 结论 + 要点 + 考点 ‹ 1 一块银白色的小金属，为什么必须泡在煤油里，着火时连水都不能浇？ 整体 · 一张实验台上把「怎么放、怎么烧、遇水怎样、着火怎么办」走一遍 最外层 1 个电子 四个站位 0.0 mmol 动手试一试 还没做 拖动视角，绕这张实验台看一圈（滚轮拉近拉远） 应该看到：四个站位都在：① 玻璃片上的钠 + 煤油瓶里泡着的钠（对照）、② 坩埚 + 酒精灯 + 常温对照钠、③ 两只烧杯 + 绿豆大钠、④ 陶土盘 + 三种灭火器材；⑤ 视窗悬在上方。主读数 0.0 mmol，现象「银白色金属光泽（刚切开）」 揭示结论 复位本步 四个站位 + 一个示意放大 ① 观察 › ② 氧气 › ③ 水 › ④ 扑救 › ⑤ 放大 中控台 动一个控件，钠块的颜色、火焰、读数与风险一起变 › 已转移电子 n(e⁻) 0.0 现象 — 教材 p.36 放出 H₂ — 标准状况 溶液的 pH — 课件设定 当前站位 四个站 在空气中放置的时间 0 s 150 s 300 s 灭火方式 干沙土 CO₂ 钠块质量（绿豆大 = 0.20 g） 参考 0.2 g 量程 0.1–2 g 保存在煤油中 加热（酒精灯外焰） 已滴加酚酞溶液 钠在空气里能放多久：切面光泽占比 — 放置时间 实线 敞口 · 虚线 泡在煤油里 风险指数 课件设定：钠块越大、灭火方式越错，风险越高 参考工况 开车 ① 观察站 ② 氧气站 ③ 水站 ④ 扑救站 ⑤ 示意放大（Na → Na⁺） 煤油瓶 · 钠泡在里面不变暗（对照） 生成的 H₂ 气泡 · 钠浮在水面上 三种灭火器材：干沙土 / 水 / CO₂ 灭火器 示意放大 · 正在看：③ 水站 Na 原子：最外层只有 1 个电子 Na⁺：失去 1 个电子以后 ‹ 上一步 第 1 / 9 步 下一步 › 本课是高危演示的替代：所有现象都是示意，不做爆炸特写。界面上的数字除教材常数（M(Na) = 23 g/mol、22.4 L/mol、密度 0.97 g/cm³、熔点 97.79 ℃）之外都是课件设定。第 4 步坩埚里的钠与旁边石板上的常温对照钠按示意放大到坩埚内径的 1/2（实物只有绿豆大，放大只为比色）。现象一格的五个字（浮 · 熔 · 游 · 响 · 红）是通行教学归纳（L2）：教材 p.36 只给「钠在水中的位置、钠的形状的变化、溶液颜色的变化」三个观察角度并把现象表留空，p.37 只给「剧烈反应 / 放出热量 / 溶液显碱性」三条结论。 ← → 翻步 · 点步骤条任一步可跳 · 1–9 跳步 · Esc 回中控台 快捷键：← → 翻步 · 1–9 跳步 · Q 检测 · N 设备名 · F 全屏 · Esc 回中控台 步骤 1 认识实验 2 银白变暗 3 泡在煤油里 4 加热燃烧 5 浮熔游响红 6 钠块大小 7 看进去 8 着火扑救 9 考核

probe.sample: The reflex arc Touch something hot and your hand is moving before you have thought about it. Follow the impulse through a real skeleton and nervous system. The 2D version ← Human anatomy All simulations 1 / 7 · TOUCH SOMETHING HOT Your hand jumps away The fingertips touch a hot plate. A fraction of a second later the arm has bent and the hand is off it — before you have decided anything. That is a reflex: an automatic, rapid response to a stimulus. The signal runs from a receptor in the skin to the spinal cord and straight back out to a muscle, along a path called the reflex arc. Watch for: The blue neurone carries the signal in, the red one carries it out. The purple one goes to the brain — and gets there last. The bones, nerves, spinal cord, biceps and brain are a real anatomical model. The coloured neurones are drawn along the real nerves they run in. KEY WORDS Reflex an automatic and rapid response to a stimulus, which does not involve the conscious part of the brain. Reflex arc the path the signal takes: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector. probe.sample: Digestion Starch, sugars, proteins and lipids: follow each through a real body, watch the enzymes that break them down, and see where the pieces go. Respiration ← Human anatomy All simulations 1 / 12 · THE DIGESTIVE SYSTEM An organ system that breaks food down Your digestive system is an organ system: several organs working together to digest food and absorb it. Food passes along the gut — mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine. Glands pour digestive juices into it: the salivary glands, the pancreas, and the liver, whose bile is stored in the gall bladder. Most of what you eat is large molecules — starch, proteins and lipids (fats and oils) — far too big to get into the blood. Enzymes in the digestive juices break them down into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the bloodstream. Watch for: The orange glows are food on its way through, from the mouth to the end of the large intestine. Every organ named is from the model. The model has no skin. The liver is drawn see-through so the gall bladder and pancreas behind it show. KEY WORDS Organ system a group of organs that work together to do a job. Digestion breaking large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble ones. Gland an organ that makes and releases substances, such as digestive juices. probe.head: Respiration Every cell in your body is running one chemical reaction, all the time. Follow the glucose in from your food and the oxygen in from the air, through a real body, to the cell that uses them
probe.sample: Respiration Every cell in your body is running one chemical reaction, all the time. Follow the glucose in from your food and the oxygen in from the air, through a real body, to the cell that uses them. The heart and circulation ← Human anatomy All simulations 1 / 10 · THE EQUATION Every cell needs glucose and oxygen Respiration is a chemical reaction that happens all the time in every living cell. It transfers the energy the cell needs to stay alive. It needs two things: glucose, which comes from the food you eat, and oxygen, which comes from the air you breathe in. The blood carries both to every cell — here, the cells of a thigh muscle. The reaction makes carbon dioxide and water; the carbon dioxide is carried back to the lungs and breathed out. Watch for: Gold: glucose coming in from food. Blue: oxygen coming in from air. Grey: carbon dioxide going out. Respiration is not the same as breathing. Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs; respiration is the reaction inside cells. KEY WORDS Aerobic respiration glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. "Aerobic" means it uses oxygen. Exothermic a reaction that transfers energy to its surroundings. Respiration is exothermic. Skeleton, mouth, gut, airways, bronchi, lungs, heart and thigh muscles: Z-Anatomy, CC BY-SA 4.0 (from BodyParts3D, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP). probe.sample: Cell membrane Cytoplasm Nucleus Mitochondria Ribosomes Nucleus Copying starts here A chromosome: a long, thin thread Two identical copies Chromosomes coil up The nuclear membrane breaks up Spindle fibres One chromosome: two identical copies Lined up across the middle Spindle fibres shorten One set to this end One set to that end Two new nuclei The chromosomes uncoil The membrane pinches in Two daughter cells genetically identical Every cell: the same 4 chromosomes Mitosis and the cell cycle A body cell grows, copies its chromosomes, divides its nucleus and then splits in two: interphase, mitosis and cytokinesis, round and round. ← Genetics Meiosis All simulations 1 / 8 · CYCLE The cell cycle Body cells make new cells by dividing in two. A cell that divides goes round a cycle of three stages, again and again: Stage 1 — interphase. The cell grows, makes more of its sub-cellular structures such as mitochondria and ribosomes, and copies its DNA. Stage 2 — mitosis. One set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell, and the nucleus divides. Stage 3 — cytokinesis. The cytoplasm and cell membrane divide, making two identical cells. Look for: The pie chart is drawn to scale. Interphase takes about 23 hours of a 24-hour cycle; mitosis and cytokinesis together take about an hour. That is why most cells you see down a microscope are in interphase. Different kinds of cell take different times. KEY WORDS Cell cycle the series of stages a cell goes through as it grows and divides. Cycle times: a typical human cell dividing in a lab, about once a day. Different cells take different times. A human body cell has 46 chromosomes, in 23 pairs. Gametes — sperm and egg cells — are different. They have just one chromosome from each pair: 23 in a human. They are made by a special kind of cell division, meiosis, in the reproductive organs: the testes and the ovaries. At fertilisation a sperm and an egg join, and the full number is restored. Look for: This cell has 4 chromosomes in 2 pairs. Follow the diagram: copied once, divided twice, giving 4 gametes with 2 chromosomes each. Mitosis makes two cells, each identical to the parent. Meiosis makes four, each with half the number of chromosomes, and all different. KEY WORDS Gamete a sex cell: a sperm cell or an egg cell. Meiosis cell division that makes gametes. The cell divides twice, making four gametes, each with a single set of chromosomes. Everything here is drawn, not photographed: real chromosomes are not coloured by where they came from. probe.head: Moles: Mr first, then a ratio Help for Chemsheets GCSE 1092. Every question on this sheet is the same two moves. Work out the relative formula mass. Then set up a ratio and cross-multiply. You never n
probe.sample: Moles: Mr first, then a ratio Help for Chemsheets GCSE 1092. Every question on this sheet is the same two moves. Work out the relative formula mass. Then set up a ratio and cross-multiply. You never need to remember a triangle or which way round a formula goes — the ratio tells you. The one fact The ratio method Units Sig figs Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4 Q5 Cheat sheet The one fact this whole sheet rests on Mr grams of a substance is exactly 1 mole of it. Mr of water is 18, so 18 g of water is 1 mole of water. Mr of carbon dioxide is 44, so 44 g of CO2 is 1 mole of CO2. That single sentence is the bridge between grams (what a balance shows you) and moles (how chemists count particles). Everything else on the sheet is proportion: if 18 g is 1 mole, then 36 g is 2 moles, 9 g is 0.5 moles, 90 g is 5 moles. It works because of how the mole was defined. One mole is 6.022 × 1023 particles, and that number was chosen precisely so that this comes out tidy. If that is new, the Avogadro constant page covers it. So step one is always the same: work out Mr. Until you have that number you cannot start. If you are shaky on it, do the relative formula mass page first. The ratio method Once you have Mr, write down two rows. The top row is the fact you just worked out. The bottom row is what the question actually gives you, with a ? where the answer goes. Worked example: how many moles are there in 90.0 g of H2O? STEP 1 · MR Element Atoms Ar Mass H hydrogen 2 1 2 × 1 = 2 O oxygen 1 16 1 × 16 = 16 Mr of H2O 18 STEP 2 · SET UP THE RATIO MASS IN GRAMS MOLES what M r tells you 18 1 what the question says 90.0 ? Cross-multiply Show it all Why cross-multiplying is safe. The two columns are in proportion, so the two diagonal products are always equal. That is true whichever box is empty — which is why the same setup answers "find the moles", "find the mass" and even "find the Mr". You do not have to decide whether to multiply or divide before you start. Set it up, cross-multiply, then rearrange. The top row always has a 1 in the moles column. That is the whole point of Mr: it is the mass of exactly one mole. Check it looks sensible Before you write the answer down, ask which number should be bigger. If the mass is… then the number of moles is… bigger than Mr grams (90 g of water, Mr 18) more than 1 mole (5 moles) ✓ smaller than Mr grams (5.8 g of C4H10, Mr 58) less than 1 mole (0.1 moles) ✓ tiny (20.6 mg of gold, Mr 197) a very small fraction of a mole ✓ If you get 5 moles from 5.8 g of something with an Mr of 58, you have divided the wrong way round. This check catches it every time. Units: g

probe.head: The Avogadro constant, explained with shopping Help for Chemsheets GCSE 1091. Work through it from the top. Each question has a 🛒 shop version first, then the 🧪 worksheet version. The maths is the s
probe.sample: The Avogadro constant, explained with shopping Help for Chemsheets GCSE 1091. Work through it from the top. Each question has a 🛒 shop version first, then the 🧪 worksheet version. The maths is the same both times. Big idea Calculator Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4 Pattern The big idea: a mole is just a pack size In a shop, eggs come in boxes of 12. We call 12 things a dozen. Chemists count atoms in packs too. But atoms are so tiny that the pack has to be enormous: 602,200,000,000,000,000,000,000 atoms. That pack is called a mole. The number in it, 6.022 × 1023, is the Avogadro constant. ▶ Play A dozen A mole 1 mole 🥚 🥚 🥚 🥚 🥚 🥚 🥚 🥚 🥚 🥚 🥚 🥚 If you counted one atom every second, it would take you about 19,000,000,000,000,000 years to count one mole. That's over a million times the age of the Universe. Translate shop → chemistry 🛒 In the shop 🧪 On the worksheet one item (one egg) one atom price of one item mass of one atom a pack of 12 (a dozen) a mole: a pack of 6.022 × 1023 how many packs you buy how many moles price of the whole lot mass of the whole lot There are only two moves ÷ You know the whole lot and want ONE. A box of 12 costs £6.00, so one costs £6.00 ÷ 12. × You know ONE and want the whole lot. One can costs 65p, so 24 cans cost 24 × 65p. Step 0, every time: count the items. number of items = number of packs × pack size number of atoms = number of moles × 6.022 × 1023 Before you start: two calculator tips Typing 6.022 × 1023. Use the ×10x button (on some calculators it's EXP or EE): type 6.022 ×10x 23. ⚠️ Dividing by it: if you type 12 ÷ 6.022 × 10^23, the calculator works out (12 ÷ 6.022) and then multiplies by 1023. That's completely wrong. Use the ×10x button, or brackets: 12 ÷ (6.022 × 10^23). Significant figures (s.f.). Start counting at the first digit that isn't zero. 45.93 to 3 s.f. → 45.9 · 0.000545 has 3 s.f. · 1.9927 × 10−23 to 3 s.f. → 1.99 × 10−23 (the ×10 part doesn't change). To type an answer into the boxes on this page, write 1.99e-23 or 1.99x10^-23. Question 1: know the whole lot, find ONE ÷ share out 1a ÷ 🛒 Shop: A box of 12 cupcakes costs £6.00. probe.head: Relative formula mass, step by step Help for Chemsheets GCSE 1411. Start with the periodic table at the top — nearly every mistake on this sheet is really a mistake about which number to read or which
probe.sample: Relative formula mass, step by step Help for Chemsheets GCSE 1411. Start with the periodic table at the top — nearly every mistake on this sheet is really a mistake about which number to read or which atoms to count. Then work down. Every answer is hidden until you press a button, so have a go first. 1. The periodic table 2. Reading a formula 3. Working out Mr Try any formula Q a–c Q d–f Cheat sheet 1. The periodic table: two numbers, and only one of them is mass Every box on the periodic table carries the same two numbers. Click any element below and look at what changes. 1 H 1 4 He 2 7 Li 3 9 Be 4 11 B 5 12 C 6 14 N 7 16 O 8 19 F 9 20 Ne 10 23 Na 11 24 Mg 12 27 Al 13 28 Si 14 31 P 15 32 S 16 35.5 Cl 17 40 Ar 18 39 K 19 40 Ca 20 45 Sc 21 48 Ti 22 51 V 23 52 Cr 24 55 Mn 25 56 Fe 26 59 Co 27 59 Ni 28 63.5 Cu 29 65 Zn 30 70 Ga 31 73 Ge 32 75 As 33 79 Se 34 80 Br 35 84 Kr 36 85 Rb 37 88 Sr 38 89 Y 39 91 Zr 40 93 Nb 41 96 Mo 42 98 Tc 43 101 Ru 44 103 Rh 45 106 Pd 46 108 Ag 47 112 Cd 48 115 In 49 119 Sn 50 122 Sb 51 128 Te 52 127 I 53 131 Xe 54 133 Cs 55 137 Ba 56 139 La 57 178.5 Hf 72 181 Ta 73 184 W 74 186 Re 75 190 Os 76 192 Ir 77 195 Pt 78 197 Au 79 201 Hg 80 204 Tl 81 207 Pb 82 209 Bi 83 209 Po 84 210 At 85 222 Rn 86 223 Fr 87 226 Ra 88 227 Ac 89 the lanthanides and actinides live here — you do not need them at GCSE 63.5 Cu 29 Copper ↑ top, bigger Ar = 63.5 — the relative atomic mass. This is the one you use. ↓ bottom, smaller 29 — the atomic number: 29 protons. Never used for mass. So one copper atom is 5.3 times as heavy as a carbon atom. Mr of Cu on its own = 63.5. The one rule to remember: the bigger number is the relative atomic mass, Ar. That is the one you use in every calculation on this sheet. The smaller number is the atomic number — how many protons. You need it for electronic structure, not for mass. Two elements where getting this wrong really shows: potassium is Ar 39 (atomic number 19), and copper is Ar 63.5 (atomic number 29). If you write 19 or 29, you have read the wrong number. What "relative" means Ar has no units. It is a comparison: a carbon-12 atom is called exactly 12, and every other atom is measured against it. So Ar = 24 for magnesium means a magnesium atom is twice as heavy as a carbon atom. That is all. A few values aren't whole numbers — chlorine is 35.5, copper 63.5. That is because a real sample is a mixture of isotopes, and the number on the table is the average. Use 35.5 exactly as it is written; do not round it to 35 or 36. 2. probe.head: Percentage by mass, explained Help for Chemsheets GCSE 1413. The question is always the same one: out of the whole compound, how much of the mass is that element? Everything you need comes off the per
probe.sample: Percentage by mass, explained Help for Chemsheets GCSE 1413. The question is always the same one: out of the whole compound, how much of the mass is that element? Everything you need comes off the periodic table. Work down the page — the answers are hidden until you press a button. The idea Off the periodic table The method Naming help Questions 1–10 Cheat sheet The idea: split the mass into slices Imagine you could weigh one formula unit of a compound and then separate it into piles, one pile per element. Percentage by mass asks how big one pile is compared with the whole thing. Here is water. Press the buttons to change which element you are asking about — the sum changes, but the picture doesn't. % by mass of H % by mass of O H 2 O 16 0 the whole compound weighs 18 The oxygen slice is 16 out of 18. Element How many atoms in the formula Ar Mass of that element H hydrogen 2 1 2 × 1 = 2 O oxygen 1 16 1 × 16 = 16 Mr of H2O — add the last column up 18 Now put the two numbers into the fraction % O = 100 × 1 × 16 = 16 18 = 88.8889 … = 88.9% (3 significant figures. Check: the other 1 element make up the remaining 11.1%.) Notice that the percentages of every element in a compound add up to 100%. That is a free check on your answers: in water, 11.1% hydrogen + 88.9% oxygen = 100%. Why hydrogen is such a small slice. Water is two hydrogens and only one oxygen — yet oxygen is nearly nine tenths of the mass. Percentage by mass is not about how many atoms there are; it is about how heavy they are. One oxygen atom (16) outweighs two hydrogens (2) eight times over. Where every number comes from There is only one source of data in this whole topic: the bigger number in each periodic table box, the relative atomic mass Ar. probe.head: A Disk on a Turntable Static friction provides the net inward force until slipping begins; then kinetic friction acts. Controls: Radius (cm): 2 23 Static Friction μs: 0.40 1.00 Kinetic Friction μk: 0.
probe.sample: A Disk on a Turntable Static friction provides the net inward force until slipping begins; then kinetic friction acts. Controls: Radius (cm): 2 23 Static Friction μs: 0.40 1.00 Kinetic Friction μk: 0.10 1.00 Angular Acceleration: 0.20 1.00 Start Pause Reset Info Status: Sticking: static friction ω: 0.00 rad/s Required fs: 0.02 N Max static: 7.85 N Kinetic fk: 5.69 N Actual friction: 0.02 N Disk on a Turntable Physics Simulation This interactive 3D physics simulation demonstrates how friction allows a disk to move in circular motion on a rotating turntable. The simulation shows the difference between static friction and kinetic friction, and it avoids treating “centripetal force” as a separate new force. Static Friction Provides the Net Inward Force While the disk sticks to the turntable, static friction supplies the force needed for the disk’s circular motion. Because the turntable has angular acceleration, static friction may have both an inward component and a tangential component. Fstatic ≤ μsN When Slipping Begins Slipping begins when the required static friction becomes larger than the maximum available static friction. At that moment, the disk no longer co-rotates with the turntable. The contact force changes from static friction to kinetic friction. Fkinetic = μkN Important Physics Idea Before slipping, the friction force is whatever value is needed to maintain circular motion, up to its maximum value. After slipping begins, friction does not become zero; it becomes kinetic friction and acts opposite the relative motion between the disk and the turntable surface. What Students Learn Static Friction Static friction adjusts its magnitude and direction to keep the disk moving with the turntable. Kinetic Friction After slipping begins, kinetic friction acts opposite the disk’s motion relative to the table. Net Inward Force The inward component of friction provides the inward acceleration needed for circular motion. Graph Interpretation The graph compares the actual friction force with the maximum static friction and kinetic friction. 相关物理仿真 全部物理仿真 Disk on a Turntable Simulation | Physics Simulation

probe.head: Double Cone Rolling Uphill The cone rolls up the track, but its center of mass moves downward Controls Rolling Object Double Cone Log Can Bottle Cone Track Opening Angle α α = 25° Cone Side Angle β β
probe.sample: Double Cone Rolling Uphill The cone rolls up the track, but its center of mass moves downward Controls Rolling Object Double Cone Log Can Bottle Cone Track Opening Angle α α = 25° Cone Side Angle β β = 18° Track Upward Angle γ γ = 5.0° Cone Base Radius R R = 0.80 m Friction / Energy Loss loss = 0.03 θ = geometry angle showing how much the cone’s center of mass tends to move downward θ = 8.7° Condition: γ < θ : rolls uphill Effective slope: 3.7° x = 0.00 m r = 1.44 m v = 0.00 m/s Start Reset Info Energy Distribution KE: 0.00 J PE lost: 0.00 J Thermal: 0.00 J KE PE Lost Thermal The center of mass goes down even though the cone appears to roll up. Graphs Center of Mass Height vs Position Speed vs Position Rolling Radius vs Position Double Cone Rolling Uphill Physics Simulation This interactive 3D physics simulation demonstrates the famous double cone rolling uphill or defying gravity illusion. The double cone appears to roll upward along a V-shaped track, but the actual center of mass moves downward. Why Does the Double Cone Roll Uphill? The V-shaped track becomes wider as the cone moves forward. Because the cone is thicker near the middle and narrower near the ends, the support points move outward and the center of mass can become lower even while the rails themselves rise. sin θ = tan α tan β Here, α represents the opening angle of the V-shaped track, and β represents the cone angle. The angle θ describes the effective downward direction of the center of mass when the track is flat. Condition for Rolling Against the Slope If the track is tilted upward by angle γ, the cone will still roll in the direction that looks uphill when: γ < θ In this case, the rails rise, but the center of mass decreases in height. Gravity is not violated. The motion is still caused by gravitational potential energy decreasing. Energy Conservation and Rolling Without Slipping The rolling condition connects translational and rotational motion: v = rω The effective rolling radius changes as the cone moves along the track: r = R - x tan θ As the radius becomes smaller, the cone can spin faster even if the forward speed eventually slows down. This makes the double-cone motion different from a simple cylinder rolling down a ramp. What Students Learn The apparent motion of an object can be different from the motion of its center of mass. Gravity lowers the center of mass; it does not pull the cone uphill. The V-shaped track geometry controls whether the illusion works. Rolling without slipping connects linear speed, angular speed, and effective radius. Energy conservation explains the m

Students can explore how the normal force, friction, weight, and inward net force determine the maximum speed of a car moving around a curve. Centripetal Force Is Not a Separate Force In circular motion, the centripetal force is the net inward force. It is not an additional force placed on the force diagram. For a car on a banked track, the real forces are weight, normal force, and friction. Fnet inward = mv2/r Maximum Speed on a Banked Track For the maximum-speed case, the car tends to slide up the bank, so friction acts down the slope. probe.head: Casimir Effect Simulation Quantum vacuum fluctuations create an attractive force between two conducting plates. Controls Plate Separation: Casimir Pressure: 1.61e-5 Pa Observation: As plate separation
probe.sample: Casimir Effect Simulation Quantum vacuum fluctuations create an attractive force between two conducting plates. Controls Plate Separation: Casimir Pressure: 1.61e-5 Pa Observation: As plate separation decreases, long wavelengths disappear inside the plates. Only shorter modes remain. Information Casimir Effect Simulation This interactive 3D physics simulation demonstrates the Casimir Effect, a quantum mechanical effect in which two closely spaced conducting plates experience an attractive force due to vacuum fluctuations. Key Physics Concept In quantum field theory, empty space is not truly empty. The vacuum contains fluctuating electromagnetic fields. When two conducting plates are placed very close together, only certain wavelengths of vacuum fluctuation can exist between the plates. P = −π²ℏc / (240a⁴) Here, P is the Casimir pressure, ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, c is the speed of light, and a is the separation between the plates. How to Use the Simulation Adjust the plate separation. Observe the vacuum fluctuation particles inside and outside the plates. Watch the force arrows showing attraction between the plates. Notice that the pressure increases rapidly as the plate separation becomes smaller. What Students Learn Vacuum Fluctuations The quantum vacuum contains fluctuating fields, even when no ordinary particles are present. Allowed Modes Between Plates The conducting plates restrict the wavelengths that can exist between them, producing an imbalance between inside and outside vacuum modes. Attractive Quantum Force The imbalance in vacuum pressure produces a small attractive force between the plates. Strong Distance Dependence The Casimir pressure varies as 1/a⁴, so the effect becomes much stronger when the plates are very close together. Frequently Asked Questions What is the Casimir Effect? The Casimir Effect is the attraction between closely spaced conducting plates caused by quantum vacuum fluctuations. Is empty space really empty? In quantum mechanics, empty space still contains fluctuating fields. These vacuum fluctuations can produce measurable effects. Why do the plates attract? The plates restrict electromagnetic modes between them. This creates a pressure difference between the inside and outside regions, leading to attraction. Why does the force increase at small separation? The Casimir pressure depends on the fourth power of the inverse separation, so reducing the distance greatly increases the force. Controls: Mass (kg): 0.2 5.0 Radius (m): 1 6 Speed (m/s): 0.5 6.0 ω = 0.67 rad/s Period = 9.42 s Fnet inward = 1.60 N Tension T = Fnet inward Start Pause Reset Info Student: Answer Fnet: Check Net Inward Force and Circular Motion Simulation This interactive 3D physics simulation explains circular motion without introducing a false extra force. The simulation shows that the inward component of the net force causes the centripetal acceleration. Centripetal Acceleration Is Caused by Net Force For uniform circular motion, the speed is constant and the acceleration points toward the center of the circle. Therefore, the net force also points inward. Fnet inward = m v2 / r There Is No New Force Called Fc The phrase “centripetal force” should not be treated as a new force. It means the inward component of the net force. The real forces may be tension, friction, normal force, gravity, or a combination of forces. This Simulation Example: Tension In this simulation, a ball moves in a circle because the string pulls inward. The tension in the string provides the inward net force. T = Fnet inward = m v2 / r Important Note About Non-Uniform Circular Motion If the speed is changing, there is tangential acceleration. In that case, the total net force does not point exactly toward the center; it has both radial and tangential components. What Students Learn Net Force The inward net force causes the inward acceleration in uniform circular motion. Tension In this example, tension is the real force that points inward. Speed and Radius Increasing speed increases the required inward force; increasing radius decreases it. Correct Force Diagrams Do not add a separate “centripetal force” arrow unless it represents the net inward force. 相关物理仿真 全部物理仿真 Net Inward Force and Circular Motion Simulation | 乐启享物理仿真

Kinetic friction does negative work and converts mechanical energy into thermal energy. This is a sliding block model: friction converts mechanical energy into thermal energy. Conservation of Energy on an Inclined Ramp Simulation This interactive 3D physics simulation demonstrates the principle of conservation of energy using a block moving up an inclined ramp with friction. It is designed to help students understand the work–energy theorem, including the relationships between kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy, thermal energy, and non-conservative work. Energy Transformation on an Inclined Plane As the block moves upward along the ramp, its initial kinetic energy is gradually converted into gravitational potential energy. At the same time, kinetic friction does negative work on the system, transforming part of the mechanical energy into thermal energy. Energy Equation for Motion on a Ramp The total energy transformation for the motion is described by: ½mv2 = mgh + μmg cos(θ)d Since the vertical height is related to the distance along the ramp by h = d sin(θ), the stopping distance becomes: d = v2 / [2g(sinθ + μcosθ)] Energy Conservation with Friction When friction is present, the mechanical energy (KE + PE) decreases as the block moves upward. However, this does not violate energy conservation. The energy lost from mechanical energy appears as thermal energy due to non-conservative work. KE + PE + Ethermal = constant What Students Learn Kinetic Energy The motion begins with kinetic energy determined by the initial speed. Gravitational Potential Energy As the block moves upward, its height increases and potential energy grows. Thermal Energy Friction converts mechanical energy into thermal energy. Energy Conservation Total energy remains constant when mechanical and thermal energy are both considered. How to Use This Physics Simulation Adjust the initial speed of the block. Change the coefficient of kinetic friction. Modify the ramp angle. Click Start to observe the motion. Compare the energy bars for kinetic, potential, thermal, and total energy. 相关物理仿真 全部物理仿真 Conservation of Energy on an Inclined Ramp Simulation | Physics Simulation

probe.head: Density - Water - Ice Water H₂O • Density anomaly (12 molecules) Temperature 20.0°C State: Liquid-like (packed) Above 4 °C: Water molecules are closely packed and move randomly, allowing the liquid to
probe.sample: Density - Water - Ice Water H₂O • Density anomaly (12 molecules) Temperature 20.0°C State: Liquid-like (packed) Above 4 °C: Water molecules are closely packed and move randomly, allowing the liquid to occupy a smaller volume and remain relatively dense. Below 4 °C (freezing transition): Hydrogen bonds force water molecules to lock into an open, ordered network. This open structure occupies a larger volume, causing the density to decrease as liquid water transforms into ice. Why this property is crucial for life on Earth: When water freezes, this open molecular structure makes ice less dense than liquid water, causing ice to float. Floating ice forms a protective, insulating layer on lakes and oceans, preventing the water below from freezing solid. This insulation allows fish, plants, and microorganisms to survive through winter, stabilizes aquatic ecosystems, and helps regulate Earth’s climate. Without this unique density anomaly of water, many freshwater environments would freeze completely, making life as we know it impossible.

probe.sample: Einstein’s Second Postulate Speed of light in vacuum is the same for all observers Observer Speed: 0.50c Start / Restart Pause / Resume Information Home Observation: A light pulse spreads outward from its source. Both observers track how far the light travels and how long it takes. Stationary frame: Distance = x, Time = t c = x / t = 1.00 (Distance and time are scaled in this simulation) Moving frame: Distance = x′, Time = t′ (both change due to motion) c′ = x′ / t′ = [γ(x - vt)]/[γ(t - vx/c²)] = c = 1.00 Although x' and t' change (via Lorentz transformation), their ratio remains the same. Conclusion: All observers measure the same speed of light: c

The curved grid illustrates spatial curvature around the Sun. However, this is only a simplified analogy. A marble rolls toward the center of a real rubber sheet because Earth's gravity pulls it downward. Therefore, the model uses gravity to illustrate gravity rather than explaining its origin. In general relativity, gravity arises from the curvature of four-dimensional spacetime, not just space.

Ground observer: Standing at the midpoint on the ground. Relativity Result Ground frame S: Rear strike time: t = 0 Front strike time: t = 0 Therefore: simultaneous Train frame S′: Lorentz time: t′ = γ(t − vx/c²) Front strike: t′ (front) = -10.39 units Rear strike: t′ (rear) = +10.39 units So the train observer says: front strike happened first. In the ground frame, the two lightning strikes are simultaneous. But the train observer moves toward the front flash and away from the rear flash, so the front flash reaches the train observer first.

probe.sample: ELEVATOR PHYSICS SIMULATION Simulation Controls How Does an Elevator Move? Start Pause Reset Show Graph Passenger Mass 70 kg Elevator Acceleration 1.5 m/s² Maximum Speed 4.0 m/s Newton's Second Law ΣF = ma N − mg = ma Scale reading = N Live Measurements AT REST Time 0.00 s Position 0.00 m Velocity 0.00 m/s Acceleration 0.00 m/s² Weight, mg 686 N Normal Force, N 686 N Scale Reading 686 N Elevator Status Elevator at rest Press Start to begin How to Use the Elevator Physics Simulation Use this simulation to investigate elevator motion, Newton's Second Law, normal force, apparent weight, velocity, and acceleration. A useful way to study the motion is to pause the elevator during each stage and compare the normal force N with the passenger's weight mg. 1. Set the Elevator Conditions Set the Passenger Mass. Set the Elevator Acceleration. Set the Maximum Speed. Click Start to begin the elevator motion. 2. Pause at Each Stage Use the Pause button to stop the elevator temporarily during different stages of its motion. Try to pause while the elevator is: Accelerating upward Moving upward at constant velocity Slowing down near the top At each stage, compare the live measurements for normal force, weight, velocity, and acceleration. 3. Compare Normal Force and Weight N − mg = ma Observe the relationship between the normal force exerted by the elevator floor and the passenger's weight. When the elevator accelerates upward, N > mg. When acceleration is zero, N = mg. When acceleration is downward, N < mg. Because the scale measures the normal force, the scale reading is the passenger's apparent weight. 4. Study the Motion Graphs Click Show Graph to display the motion graph. Switch among: Position vs. Time Velocity vs. Time Acceleration vs. Time Pause the simulation and compare the shape of each graph with the current elevator motion and the live numerical values. What to Observe During One Elevator Trip Elevator Stage Acceleration Normal Force vs. Weight Passenger Feels At rest before starting a = 0 N = mg Normal weight Accelerating upward Upward N > mg Heavier Moving upward at constant speed a = 0 N = mg Normal weight Moving upward but slowing down Downward N < mg Lighter Stopped at the top a = 0 N = mg Normal weight Suggested Investigation: Run the elevator several times using different passenger masses and different elevator accelerations. Use the Pause button during the accelerating and decelerating stages. Record the values of mg, N, and a. Then check whether your measurements satisfy: N − mg = ma Related Physics Simulations Heat Transfer 全部物理仿真

probe.sample: Noether's Theorem Simulation Symmetry → Conservation Law Controls Mode Time Translation → Energy Space Translation → Momentum Rotation → Angular Momentum Transformation amount 1.50 Symmetry-breaking strength 0.00 Speed 1.00 Pause Reset Hide Ghost Information Symmetry preserved Current scene: A cyan block oscillates on a spring. The yellow ghost block shows the same motion after a shift in time. Meaning: The two blocks are at different positions because one motion is viewed at a later or earlier time. If the physics is unchanged by shifting time, then time-translation symmetry is present. Conserved quantity: Total energy is conserved (kinetic energy + potential energy). Energy Graph Symmetry: Time translation symmetry Conserved quantity: Energy = 4.3200 Kinetic term: 0.0000 Potential term: 4.3200 Transformation effect: Δ ≈ 0.0000 Status: Energy conserved Noether idea: same laws after transformation → conserved quantity. Noether's Theorem Simulation: Symmetry and Conservation Laws This interactive 3D physics simulation demonstrates Noether's theorem, one of the deepest ideas in modern physics. Emmy Noether showed that every continuous symmetry of the laws of physics corresponds to a conserved quantity. Main Ideas in the Simulation 1. Time translation symmetry: if the laws of physics do not change with time, energy is conserved. 2. Space translation symmetry: if the laws of physics do not change from one place to another, momentum is conserved. 3. Rotational symmetry: if the laws of physics do not change under rotation, angular momentum is conserved. 4. Symmetry breaking: when a symmetry is disturbed, the related conservation law can fail. Noether's theorem connects symmetry and conservation law: Continuous symmetry → Conserved quantity Physics Meaning In the simulation, the cyan object shows the original physical system and the yellow ghost object shows a transformed version of the same system. When the transformation does not change the physics, the symmetry is preserved and the related quantity stays nearly constant. The graph on the right shows energy, momentum, or angular momentum depending on the selected mode. How to Use This Simulation Select time, space, or rotation symmetry from the mode menu. Adjust the transformation amount to compare the original and transformed system. Increase the symmetry-breaking strength to see conservation law failure. Use the graph to observe whether the conserved quantity stays constant. Why Noether's Theorem Is Important Noether's theorem explains why conservation laws exist. probe.sample: Energy Conservation Pendulum Simulation Drag the pendulum bob and release it. Watch PE, KE, thermal energy, and total energy. Controls Mass (kg): 0.1 1.5 Gravity (m/s²): Low High Planet: Moon Mars Earth Jupiter Saturn Mercury Custom Friction / Damping: None Lots Angle: Pause Reset Info PE KE Thermal Total PE: 0.0000 J KE: 0.0000 J Thermal: 0.0000 J Mechanical: 0.0000 J Total: 0.0000 J System Idea Gravitational potential energy belongs to the Earth + pendulum bob system, not the bob alone. With friction, mechanical energy decreases, but that energy is transferred into thermal energy by non-conservative work. With no friction, PE and KE transform into each other. Mechanical energy is conserved. Energy Conservation Pendulum Simulation This interactive 3D physics simulation demonstrates the law of conservation of energy using a pendulum. Students can explore the transformation between gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, and thermal energy. System Definition in Energy Conservation A key idea in energy conservation is the definition of the system. For a pendulum, gravitational potential energy is not a property of the bob alone. It belongs to the interaction between the Earth and the pendulum bob. Therefore, the gravitational potential energy is defined for the Earth + bob system. PE = mgh Mechanical Energy Without Friction When friction is zero, the pendulum continuously transforms energy between potential energy and kinetic energy. At the highest point, potential energy is maximum and kinetic energy is minimum. At the lowest point, kinetic energy is maximum and potential energy is minimum. Emechanical = PE + KE = constant Energy Conservation With Friction When friction or air resistance is present, the mechanical energy of the pendulum decreases. However, the energy does not disappear. It is transferred to thermal energy by non-conservative work. For the larger system including the surroundings, the total energy remains conserved. PE + KE + Ethermal = constant What Students Learn Potential Energy Requires a System Gravitational potential energy is associated with the Earth-bob interaction, not only the bob by itself. Kinetic and Potential Energy Transform As the pendulum swings downward, potential energy decreases and kinetic energy increases. As it swings upward, kinetic energy decreases and potential energy increases. Friction Transfers Energy Friction reduces mechanical energy, but the lost mechanical energy appears as thermal energy. probe.head: Grangier Experiment: Proof of the Existence of Photons Controls Start Pause Experiment Theory Reset Photon Counts Triggered trials 0 Detector D1 0(0.0%) Detector D2 0(0.0%) D1 & D2 coincidences 0 g(2)
probe.sample: Grangier Experiment: Proof of the Existence of Photons Controls Start Pause Experiment Theory Reset Photon Counts Triggered trials 0 Detector D1 0(0.0%) Detector D2 0(0.0%) D1 & D2 coincidences 0 g(2)(0) 0.000 Single photons go to one output or the other. Idealized simulation: detector inefficiency, background counts, and accidental coincidences are neglected. Grangier Experiment: Proof of the Existence of Photons This interactive 3D quantum physics simulation models the Grangier–Roger–Aspect photon anticorrelation experiment. A heralded photon travels to a 50/50 beam splitter and is detected at either detector D1 or detector D2. The simulation counts detector events and D1–D2 coincidences so students can explore the nonclassical behavior of single-photon light. Key idea: an ideal single photon is detected at one output of the beam splitter or the other, not simultaneously at both outputs. Suppression of D1–D2 coincidence events is called photon anticorrelation. Second-Order Correlation g(2)(0) The detector statistics can be represented by the zero-delay second-order correlation. In this idealized simulation the displayed estimator is g(2)(0) = (N0N12) / (N1N2) Here, N0 is the number of triggered trials, N1 and N2 are the detector counts, and N12 is the number of D1–D2 coincidence events. For an ideal single-photon source in this model, N12 = 0 and therefore g(2)(0) = 0. Values below 1 indicate photon antibunching or anticorrelation and are incompatible with a simple classical description of the detected field. How to Use the Simulation Click Start to begin producing heralded photon pairs. Watch the trigger photon travel to detector D0. Follow the partner photon to the 50/50 beam splitter. Observe whether the photon is detected by D1 or D2. Compare the D1 and D2 percentages as more events accumulate. Watch the coincidence count and g(2)(0). Use Pause/Resume to inspect the apparatus and Reset to start a new run. Drag the scene to rotate the 3D view and use the mouse wheel to zoom. What Students Should Observe Random 50/50 Beam-Splitter Outcomes Each signal photon is randomly transmitted or reflected by the 50/50 beam splitter. probe.sample: Controls Induction Coil Voltage Spark Gap Distance Wave Speed Display Start Pause Reset Info Experiment Readout Voltage: 7 Spark gap: 3.6 mm EM wave: ready, speed 1.0x Receiver spark: waiting Hertz Experiment Simulation: Discovery of Electromagnetic Waves 1887 This interactive 3D physics simulation demonstrates the famous Hertz experiment. Heinrich Hertz used a spark gap transmitter and a receiver loop to confirm Maxwell’s prediction that electromagnetic waves exist and can travel through space. Main Parts of the Hertz Experiment 1. Induction coil: produces a high voltage across the spark gap. 2. Spark gap transmitter: creates a rapidly changing current when a spark jumps between two metal spheres. 3. Electromagnetic waves: spread outward from the transmitter through space. 4. Resonator receiver loop: detects the electromagnetic wave by producing a small spark across its gap. Electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light: c = 299 792 458 m/s Physics Meaning Maxwell’s theory predicted that changing electric fields and changing magnetic fields support each other and travel as electromagnetic waves. Hertz confirmed this idea experimentally. In this simulation, the spark gap acts as a transmitter. The receiver loop acts as a detector. When the wave reaches the loop, it induces an electric current, and a small spark appears at the receiver gap. Why Hertz’s Experiment Was Important Hertz’s experiment provided direct evidence that electromagnetic waves are real. This discovery became the foundation for radio, television, radar, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cell phones, and modern wireless communication. How to Use This Simulation Increase the induction coil voltage to create a stronger spark. Change the spark gap distance and observe when waves are produced. Use the wave speed display to make the spreading electromagnetic wave easier to see. Watch the receiver loop produce a small spark when the transmitted wave is detected. Educational Notes In the real Hertz experiment, electromagnetic waves are invisible and spread outward through space. In this simulation, the waves are drawn as horizontal expanding wavefronts so students can clearly visualize wave propagation from the spark-gap transmitter to the receiver loop. 相关物理仿真 RC AC Circuit Simulation 全部物理仿真 Newton’s Second Law Simulation | Physics Simulation

Hooke’s Law and Spring Motion Hooke’s Law states that the restoring force of a spring is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium: F = -kx The mass oscillates around its equilibrium position. Students can adjust amplitude, spring constant, mass, and friction to observe how each parameter affects the motion. Damping and Air Resistance The friction slider represents air resistance. When friction is increased, the oscillation amplitude gradually decreases because mechanical energy is converted into thermal energy. F_d = -bv A larger damping coefficient causes the motion to die out faster. With little or no friction, the spring-mass system behaves more like ideal simple harmonic motion. Energy Transformation The simulation includes colorful vertical energy bars showing kinetic energy, spring potential energy, total mechanical energy, and thermal heat energy. Kinetic Energy: greatest near the equilibrium position. Spring Potential Energy: greatest near the turning points. Mechanical Energy: decreases when damping is present. Thermal Heat Energy: increases as friction removes mechanical energy. E_total = KE + PE + E_thermal Real-Time Graphs A graph panel displays energy versus time and a phase-space graph of displacement versus velocity. These graphs help students connect the visible spring motion with mathematical models of oscillation and damping. What Students Learn How spring constant affects oscillation frequency and period. probe.sample: Controls Ring Type Solid ring Slit ring Solid ring after dipping in LN₂ Power Source DC AC Solid ring: small jump. Slit ring: no jump. LN₂-cooled ring: stronger jump. Start Reset Info Experiment Readout Ring: Solid ring Power source: DC Jump height: 0.0 simulation scale Velocity: 0.0 Result: brief induction pulse — small jump Jumping Ring Simulation: Thomson Ring, Faraday's Law, and Lenz's Law This interactive 3D physics simulation demonstrates the jumping ring experiment, also called the Thomson ring experiment. A conducting ring is placed above a coil with an iron core. When the current in the coil changes, the changing magnetic flux induces current in the ring and creates magnetic repulsion. Main Parts of the Jumping Ring Experiment 1. Coil and iron core: create a strong magnetic field through the ring. 2. Conducting ring: carries induced current when magnetic flux changes. 3. Power source: compares AC and DC behavior in electromagnetic induction. 4. Liquid nitrogen beaker: represents cooling the ring to reduce resistance. Faraday's law of induction: emf = - dΦ / dt Physics Meaning The minus sign in Faraday's law represents Lenz's law. The induced current produces a magnetic field that opposes the change in magnetic flux. In the jumping ring experiment, this opposition appears as an upward magnetic force on the ring. A closed conducting ring can jump because current can circulate. A slit ring has no complete path for large induced current, so it barely jumps. AC vs DC AC changes continuously, so the magnetic flux through the ring keeps changing. This produces a stronger and more sustained induced current. DC produces a brief induction effect mainly when the switch is turned on or off; after the current becomes steady, the magnetic flux no longer changes and induction stops. Liquid Nitrogen Effect Cooling the ring lowers its electrical resistance. Lower resistance allows a larger induced current for the same changing magnetic flux. As a result, the magnetic repulsion is stronger and the ring can jump higher. How to Use This Simulation Select a solid ring, slit ring, or LN₂-cooled solid ring. Choose AC or DC power and click Start. Observe the ring height and compare the readout for each case. Use Reset to return the ring to the starting position. Educational Notes In a real jumping ring demonstration, the magnetic field is invisible. In this simulation, the moving ring, coil, power supply, and readouts help students connect the visible jump to induced emf, magnetic flux, and Lenz's law. 相关物理仿真 RC AC Circuit Simulation Newton’s Second Law Simulation | Ph

probe.head: Boat Braking - Kinematic Equations Initial Speed (m/s): 4 20 Distance to Log (m): 10 50 Braking Time (s): 2 8 Speed (m/s) Distance (m) Time (s) Start Problem Formula Reset Boat Braking Exercise Studen
probe.sample: Boat Braking - Kinematic Equations Initial Speed (m/s): 4 20 Distance to Log (m): 10 50 Braking Time (s): 2 8 Speed (m/s) Distance (m) Time (s) Start Problem Formula Reset Boat Braking Exercise Student's name: Acceleration (m/s²): Does the boat stop in time? Select Yes No Check Answer Boat Braking and Constant Acceleration This interactive 3D physics simulation models a boat traveling in a straight buoy-marked channel. The boat first moves at constant speed. When the driver reaches the braking point, a floating log is a specified distance ahead, so the boat must decelerate rather than turn away. During the braking part of the motion, the boat slows uniformly from its initial speed to rest in the selected braking time: 0 = v₀ + at Therefore, the braking acceleration is: a = −v₀ / t The stopping distance is the average speed multiplied by the braking time: dstop = ½v₀t How to Use the Simulation Choose the boat's initial speed. Choose the distance from the braking point to the floating log. Choose the time from the start of braking to the log's position. Click Start. The boat first cruises at constant speed, then begins braking. Calculate the acceleration to the nearest tenth of a meter per second squared. Decide whether the boat stops in time and check both answers. What Students Learn Constant Velocity Before Braking The first part of the animation separates uniform motion from accelerated motion. The displayed braking distance and time begin when the boat starts decelerating. Negative Acceleration When acceleration is opposite the boat's velocity, the boat slows down. A negative acceleration does not automatically mean an object is slowing down; the velocity direction must also be considered. Stopping Before an Obstacle Compare the calculated stopping distance with the available distance to the log. If the stopping distance is smaller, the boat stops with water still remaining between it and the log. Example Suppose a boat begins braking at 10 m/s, the log is 30 m ahead, and the braking time is 4.0 s. a = −10 / 4 = −2.5 m/s² The stopping distance is: dstop = ½(10)(4) = 20 m The boat therefore stops 10 m before the log. probe.sample: Runway Takeoff - Kinematic Equations Controls Runway Length (m): 500 4000 Throttle Acceleration (m/s²): 0.5 5.0 Takeoff Velocity (m/s): 40 100 Speed (m/s): Distance (m): Time (s): Start Problem Formula Reset Runway Takeoff Exercise Student's name: Minimum runway required (m): Safe takeoff? Select Yes No Check Answer Runway Takeoff and Constant Acceleration This interactive 3D physics simulation models a jet accelerating from rest along an airport runway. Adjust the runway length, throttle acceleration, and required takeoff velocity to determine whether the aircraft can safely reach takeoff speed before the end of the runway. v² = v₀² + 2aΔx Because the jet starts from rest, v₀ = 0. The minimum distance required to reach takeoff speed is therefore: Δx = v² / (2a) How to Use the Simulation Adjust the runway length. Adjust the jet's constant throttle acceleration. Choose the required takeoff velocity. Click Start to watch the jet accelerate. Calculate the minimum runway distance and check your answer. What Students Learn Effect of Acceleration A greater acceleration allows the jet to reach the required takeoff velocity in a shorter distance. Effect of Takeoff Velocity The required runway distance depends on the square of the takeoff velocity. Increasing the required velocity can greatly increase the distance needed for takeoff. Runway Safety A runway is long enough only when the available runway length is greater than or equal to the distance needed for the jet to reach takeoff speed. Example For a jet accelerating from rest at 1.8 m/s² and requiring a takeoff velocity of 76 m/s: Δx = 76² / (2 × 1.8) = 1404.4 m A 1600 m runway is therefore long enough, leaving 195.6 m of runway when the aircraft reaches takeoff speed. probe.head: Interference / Fringe Shift: White = current intensity pattern. Cyan dashed = reference center. Ether ON: small shift appears during rotation. Ether OFF: no measurable shift. Michelson-Morley Experime
probe.sample: Interference / Fringe Shift: White = current intensity pattern. Cyan dashed = reference center. Ether ON: small shift appears during rotation. Ether OFF: no measurable shift. Michelson-Morley Experiment Start Rotation Rotate 15° Pause Reset Ether: OFF About Experiment Mode: Null result / no ether Angle: 0.0° Expected fringe shift: 0.000 Interpretation: No shift as apparatus rotates. Key idea: A light beam is split into two perpendicular arms. The two beams reflect from mirrors, return to the beam splitter, and recombine to form interference fringes. If Earth moved through a stationary ether, the round-trip times in the two arms should change as the apparatus rotates. Historical result: Michelson and Morley expected a fringe shift if ether wind existed. The observed result was essentially zero shift, which helped undermine the ether idea and later supported Einstein’s relativity.

probe.head: Veterinarian and Monkey Problem Projectile motion: the tranquilizer dart and monkey fall with the same acceleration g. Controls Problem Start Pause Reset Rifle Angle Slider angle = 60.0° Bullet speed
probe.sample: Veterinarian and Monkey Problem Projectile motion: the tranquilizer dart and monkey fall with the same acceleration g. Controls Problem Start Pause Reset Rifle Angle Slider angle = 60.0° Bullet speed = 40 m/s Monkey height = 63.5 m Horizontal distance = 80 m Information Check Answer Student name: Enter aiming angle (1 decimal place): ° Check Answer Hunter and Monkey Projectile Motion Simulation This interactive 3D physics simulation demonstrates the classic The Veterinarian and Monkey problem. A tranquilizer dart is fired at a monkey at the same instant the monkey begins to fall. The simulation shows why the tranquilizer dart hits the monkey when the rifle is aimed directly at the monkey’s initial position. Physics Principle The key idea is that both the tranquilizer dart and the monkey experience the same downward gravitational acceleration. Gravity causes both objects to fall by the same vertical distance during the same time interval. y = y₀ + v₀y t - ½gt² Because the tranquilizer dart and monkey both have the same gravitational term, the downward displacement caused by gravity cancels when comparing their relative vertical motion. What Students Learn Projectile motion has independent horizontal and vertical components. Gravity affects both the tranquilizer dart and the monkey equally. The rifle should be aimed directly at the monkey’s initial position. The required bullet speed must be large enough to reach the monkey before it hits the ground. Classroom Questions Would the answer change if the monkey were bigger or smaller? Would the answer change if the tranquilizer dart speed changed? What is the minimum bullet speed needed before the monkey reaches the ground? Related Mechanics Simulations Heat Transfer 全部物理仿真 Hunter and Monkey Physics Simulation | 乐启享物理仿真

probe.sample: STUDENT LEARNING ASSISTANT THIS CALCULATOR CAN SOLVE ALL OF ABOVE PROBLEMS AND MORE Students can use this calculator to check homework solutions Look at the following picture to know the names of all variables Enter all given information from the problem into boxes correctly (VERY IMPORTANT). Unit of length is meter, unit of time is second, angle is in degree. For vertical projectile motion, alpha is 90 degrees. For free fall, alpha is -90 degrees. Zero values in outputs means these values are not required to be computed: Initial height ho: Initial velocity vo: Initial angle alpha: The maximum height H: Horizontal Range R: Horizontal Range at point P (Rp): The height at point P (hp): Speed at ground (vg): Speed at point P (vp): Time to reach point P (tp): Time to reach maximum height (tmax): Time to hit the ground (tg): Angle beta (for any point P): Solve the problem The Projectile Trajectory Darker trajectory means slower motion. Reset Home This 3D physics simulation shows how mechanical advantage, efficiency, input force, and weight affect lifting. Pulley System Simulation This free interactive 3D physics simulation demonstrates how pulley systems help lift heavy objects. Students can explore fixed pulleys, movable pulleys, and compound pulley systems while observing the relationship between input force, weight, efficiency, and mechanical advantage. Key Physics Concept: Mechanical Advantage A pulley system can reduce the input force needed to lift an object by distributing the load across multiple supporting rope segments. The more supporting rope segments a system has, the greater the ideal mechanical advantage. MA = Load / Effort In an ideal pulley system, the mechanical advantage is approximately equal to the number of rope segments supporting the load. Fin = W / MA Efficiency in Real Pulley Systems Real pulley systems are not perfectly efficient because of friction, pulley weight, and energy loss. When efficiency is less than 100%, the input force must be larger than the ideal value. Fin = W / (MA × efficiency) How to Use the Simulation Select an ideal pulley or a pulley system with pulley weight. Choose one fixed pulley, one movable pulley, or a compound pulley system. Adjust the input force, weight, and efficiency. Observe when the object begins to lift. Compare the pulling distance with the lifted distance. What Students Learn Fixed Pulley A fixed pulley changes the direction of the applied force, but it does not reduce the required input force in an ideal system. Movable Pulley A movable pulley reduces the input force because the load is supported by more than one rope segment. Compound Pulley System A compound pulley system combines fixed and movable pulleys to increase mechanical advantage and make lifting easier. Efficiency Lower efficiency means more input force is required because some energy is lost to friction and pulley motion. Frequently Asked Questions What is a pulley? A pulley is a simple machine made of a wheel and a rope or cable. It helps lift objects by changing the direction of force and, in some systems, reducing the input force needed. Measure Beam Mass: Instructions and Physics This interactive 3D physics simulation demonstrates how the mass of a uniform beam can be determined using a known object and the principle of rotational equilibrium. 1. Objective Determine the unknown mass of a uniform beam by adjusting the position and mass of a known object and the position of the pivot until the beam is in rotational equilibrium. 2. How to Use the Simulation Adjust the Object Position slider to move the red object along the beam. Adjust the Object Mass slider to change the known mass. Adjust the Pivot Position to move the support point. Use the +/− buttons for precise adjustment. Normal click: 0.01; Shift + click: 0.0001. Observe the beam rotation and net torque. Continue adjusting until the net torque is approximately zero. Record the object mass, object position, and pivot position. Calculate the unknown beam mass using the rotational equilibrium equation. 3. Torque and Sign Convention Torque describes the turning effect of a force about a pivot. τ = r × F For this experiment: Counterclockwise torque is positive (+). Clockwise torque is negative (−). The net torque is zero at rotational equilibrium. Στ = 0 4. Determining the Unknown Beam Mass Let xO represent the object position, xP the pivot position, and xB the beam's center of mass. The uniform beam extends from −20 m to +20 m, so its center of mass is at xB = 0. rO = xO − xP rB = xB − xP The gravitational torque of each mass is: τO = −rOmOg τB = −rBmBg At equilibrium: τO + τB = 0 Solving for the unknown beam mass: mB = −mO (xO − xP) / (xB − xP) Since xB = 0: mB = mO (xO − xP) / xP 5. Suggested Experiment Set the object mass to 2.00 kg. Set the object position to −10.00 m. Move the pivot until net torque is zero. Record the balanced pivot position. Calculate the unknown beam mass. probe.sample: Tunnel Diode Simulation Quantum Tunneling → Negative Resistance Controls Forward Bias Voltage 0.00 V Barrier Width 1.00 nm Doping Level High Medium High Very High Electron Animation Speed 1.00 Start Pause Reset Information Tunneling region: peak-current region A tunnel diode is a heavily doped p-n junction. Its depletion region is extremely thin, so electrons can tunnel through the barrier. I-V Characteristic Voltage: 0.00 V Current: 0.000 simulation units Region: Tunneling current increases Differential resistance: positive Tunnel Diode Simulation: Quantum Tunneling and Negative Resistance This interactive 3D physics simulation demonstrates the tunnel diode, a semiconductor device that uses quantum tunneling. Unlike an ordinary diode, a tunnel diode has a region where increasing voltage causes current to decrease. This is called negative differential resistance. Main Parts of the Tunnel Diode Simulation 1. Heavily doped p-n junction: creates an extremely thin depletion region. 2. Quantum tunneling barrier: electrons can pass through the barrier even when they do not have enough classical energy. 3. Peak current: tunneling is strongest when occupied states align with empty states. 4. Valley current: tunneling decreases after the energy states become misaligned. 5. Normal diode current: at higher forward voltage, ordinary conduction increases again. Simple tunneling idea: Tunneling probability decreases rapidly as barrier width increases. Physics Meaning In a tunnel diode, electrons behave like quantum waves. If the depletion barrier is thin enough, part of the electron wavefunction can penetrate and pass through the barrier. This produces tunneling current. At low forward bias, energy states align and current increases. At a larger bias, the states become misaligned, so tunneling current decreases. This creates the negative resistance region. Why Tunnel Diodes Are Important Tunnel diodes are famous because they show a direct technological application of quantum tunneling. Their negative resistance allows very fast switching and microwave oscillation. They are useful examples in semiconductor physics, modern physics, electronics, and quantum mechanics. How to Use This Simulation Increase the forward bias voltage and observe how current changes. Watch the I-V graph move from peak current to negative resistance and valley current. Increase the barrier width and observe that tunneling becomes weaker. Change the doping level to see how a thinner barrier increases tunneling current. probe.head: Work-Energy Simulation Work–Energy: Ramp + Friction Floor A cube starts from height h on a frictionless ramp, then slides on a horizontal floor with friction μ. Find the stopping distance d on the flo
probe.sample: Work-Energy Simulation Work–Energy: Ramp + Friction Floor A cube starts from height h on a frictionless ramp, then slides on a horizontal floor with friction μ. Find the stopping distance d on the floor. Height h: Friction μ: Your answer d: Student: Run Reset Result: Conservation of Energy and Work-Energy Principle This interactive 3D physics simulation demonstrates conservation of mechanical energy and the work-energy principle. A cube slides down a frictionless ramp, converts gravitational potential energy into kinetic energy, and then slows down on a rough horizontal surface due to friction. Key Physics Concept At the top of the ramp, the cube has gravitational potential energy. If the ramp is frictionless, this energy becomes kinetic energy at the bottom. mgh = ½mv² On the rough horizontal floor, friction does negative work and brings the cube to rest. Wfriction = − μmgd Using energy conservation and the work-energy principle: mgh = μmgd d = h / μ How to Use the Simulation Read the ramp-and-friction problem. Calculate the stopping distance using energy ideas. Enter your answer. Click Run Simulation. Compare your prediction with the simulation result. What Students Learn Energy Conversion Gravitational potential energy changes into kinetic energy as the cube slides down the frictionless ramp. Work Done by Friction On the rough floor, friction removes mechanical energy and brings the cube to rest. Mass Cancels Out The stopping distance does not depend on the mass of the cube because mass appears in both gravitational energy and friction work. Effect of Friction A larger coefficient of friction gives a shorter stopping distance, while a smaller coefficient gives a longer stopping distance. Frequently Asked Questions What is conservation of energy? Conservation of energy means energy can change form, but the total energy remains constant if no external non-conservative work is done. What is the work-energy principle? The work-energy principle states that the net work done on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy. Why does the cube stop on the horizontal floor? The cube stops because friction does negative work and removes its kinetic energy. What is the theoretical stopping distance? For height h = 10 m and μ = 0.8, the distance is d = h / μ = 10 / 0.8 = 12.5 m. Related Mechanics Simulations 全部物理仿真 Work-Energy Simulation | 乐启享物理仿真 Created by Thomas Nguyen |
